doc.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Society reporter in Chicago: Ray Nance and Lawrence Brown
summary: Covering debutante parties she heard Ray Nance and met Lawrence Brown, later honored in her memorial for him.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: At that time, jazz was the popular music, isn’t that right?

Yes. You know my first job I was a society reporter in Chicago on first The Tabloid, which is now known as the Sun Times, and then the Hearst paper. And everybody in my age group was coming out. So there were debutante parties. And it was perfect for me, because they all had wonderful bands. The first time I ever heard Ray Nance was covering a debut of a girl named Bird Littlefield in Chicago. She had a coming out party at the Blackstone Hotel. And I think there was sort of a balcony around the ballroom and off of which were the ladies cloak room and different places. I was in there taking my gloves off and I heard this sound coming up. And I went out and hung over the balcony. It was so beautiful. It was Ray Nance playing, he called it “Kitty on Toast,” it was a variation of “Honeysuckle Rose.” My gosh, it was the most gorgeous thing I’d ever heard. And there were big bands that played for — Sheila Cuttahee had Duke Ellington’s orchestra. That was about 1938 I think. And I was with a fellow called Dodge from I guess Grosse Pointe, Michigan. I guess he was a famous Dodge, I don’t know, he was my date that night. And he said, it came midnight and they’d break you know and have breakfast. That was a big thing in those days, these balls, you’d have some kind of midnight supper or something. He said, “shall we go up and sit with the band?” And they were sitting on the balcony. I said, “yes we will.” So we went and sat there, and that’s how I’ve met my dream prince of all time, that I’ve never gotten over, Lawrence Brown. And he was my favorite. And so I sat next to him and we talked. I did a memorial for him © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

at St. Peter’s Church here. And he died in California, but I thought I’d do it here, because I had a lot of stuff on him. I had slides and photographs and a lot of details. And I said at the memorial that he always looked like Rudolph Valentino to me. And I said if Rudolph Valentino could play the trombone, he’d probably sound like Lawrence.

Oh, it was so romantic. So while I was doing all this, somebody showed up with a vase with roses and put it on the lectern or whatever you call it, the pulpit. I said, “roses, this is like Rudolph Valentino.” And it was some woman’s name signed to the roses, I have no idea who it was, and so that was that. Bobby Short was a little boy who was a kiddie performer. And when he went out to California he moved in with you know, little colored kids, or any kids on the road I guess had trouble finding accommodations. And he moved in with the family of Lawrence’s brother, Harold Brown. And so he stole some pictures for me. So I have pictures of Lawrence at an early age.
